## Where we agree with eversource, and where we don't
* Eversource agrees that heat pump customers should pay close to their marginal delivery cost!
* Eversource has pointed out an important problem with its current design for R1: when the incremental load associated with a new heat pump installation is priced at higher than marginal delivery cost, heat pump customers overpay for electric delivery, and that makes heat pumps more expensive to operate than they should be, creating a barrier to adoption.
* Therefore, they propose to a special rate for heat pump customers that is aims to price the incremental load closer to marginal delivery cost.
* They still want to price it highter then marginal delivery cost, in order to put downward pressure on the total energy bill of heat pump customers.
* They frame this as a "win-win" affordability measure: as customers adopt heat pumps under the rate, their bills would be lower than without the rate, and the bills of customers who have not yet adopted the rate would also be lower.

* However, they only want to make this rate available to delivered fuel customers, who already save by switching to heat pumps under current rates. They don't want to make it available to natural gas customers, because these customers largely do not save by switching to heat pumps under current rates.
* This makes no sense.
* The company says one of their goals is to increase heat pump adoption. The biggest barrier to adoption is precisely for customers who are currently under natural gas. Those on delivered fuels do not face an operating cost barrier to adoption.
* More fundamentally, the reason that natural gas customers largely don't save when switching to heat pumps is precisely _because_ these customer are being overcharged for delivery.

## Their rate
* TABLE: proposed R1 rate vs. their propose R6
* Okay, how close is the proposed rate to this ideal? (Bearing in mind that Eversource only wants the rate to be available to delivered fuel customers, but seeing what would happen if it was also offered to heat pump customers.)
* Not close at all. It only removes TK% of the overpayment for all customers, TK% for delivered fuel customers, and TK% for heat pump customers.
* CHART: Overpayment in Eversource: incremental revenue vs. incremental marginal costs, under R1 vs. R6
* Because of that, the impact on bills when switching would be minimal. (Here's what would happen to natural gas customers.)
1. It only reduces distribution charges, not other charges, and it doesn't reduce them by enough. (Keeping the threshold constant, but lowering the other rates, you'd need a discount of TK% across them to fully remove the overpayment.)
2. But even if you remove the overpayment for the average fossi-heating customer, using a tiered design might sound like a good way to target incremental load on paper, but it's a bad for both heat pump adoption and equity in practice.
  - The idea of using the median load to set the threshold is that it's a coarse way to figure incremental load associated with the heat pump.
  - But there's a lot of variance around the median. Anyone above the median is going to get a discount on part of their base load, and all of their heat pump load. Anyone below the median is not going to get a discount on none of their base load, and not all of their heat pump load.
  - And it turns out that in CT, people who heat with natural gas used less electricity on average than people who heat with delivered fuels. So this means that customers who heat with delivered fuels—those who already have large savings when switching—will get a large discount than they should, on average, wheras those who heat with natural gas—who currently don't save when switching—will get a smaller discount than they should, on average
  - Load is correlated with income, so that means that high-income delivered fuel customers will get a larger discount than they should, on average, and the same for high-income natural gas customers.
  - So this policy is not only bad for heat pump adoption, it's also bad for equity. It gives bigger discounts to people who need them less.
  - Physical or virtual sub-metering of the heat pump would fix this. A partial solution would simply be to use one median for customers coming from natural gas, and another for customers coming from delivered fuels. But this would require knowing which customers are coming from which fuel, which Eversource does not.

## Our rate

* Okay, so we've learned that Eversource have the right premises but the wrong conclusions: it's true that heat pump customers are being overcharged, but it's false that heat pump customers should not be offered access to fair rates on the grounds of ending up with higher bills, because the main reason they end up with higher bills is that they've being overcharged for delivery.
* We know that fully removing the overpayment for all customers would transform the economics of heat pump operations, especially for customers coming from natural gas.
* So, how would we do this in practice?

* I. Individualized metering
* Actually achieving this rate would require a separate meter for the heat pumps, though you could do an approximation in billing software to only target the incremental load of each individual home.


* II. Next best thing: a seasonal rate
* But short of this, you can get nearly the same effect through a simple seasonal rate available to all customers, which we present here.

## Implementation
* You need to do auto-enrollment or this doesn't matter.
* BTW this is what Mass did.
* Key point: auto-enrolling existing customers has bill impacts on others, auto-enrolling new customers does not.
* However, because there are so few existing heat pump customers, the impact on others is very small. (It would be even smaller in practice, because Eversource is only aware of TK% of its customers with heat pumps.)

### Hourly marginal distribution costs {#sec-method-dist-mc}

The distribution and sub-transmission marginal cost series shown in @fig-mc-heatmap-dist-sub-tx is an hourly schedule covering all 8,760 hours of 2025, built in four steps.

**Step 1: Annualized marginal capacity cost.** We used the system-wide annualized marginal distribution station and trunkline feeder cost of **$20.17/kW-year** (2026 dollars) from Table 3 of Eversource's marginal cost of service study (MCOS), filed in its 2026 rate case, Docket 26-05-10 [@eversource_Docket260510Exhibit_2026; @eversource_Docket260510Exhibit_2026a] [[p. 7](https://www.documentcloud.org/documents/28540599-exhibit-clp-mcos-2/#document/p7/a2826034)]. This is the system-wide average — Eversource diluted the locational cost in expansion areas ($86.58/kW-year) by the share of system peak load in those areas — and covers upstream distribution only (substations and primary trunkline feeders).

**Step 2: CPI adjustment.** We deflated $20.17/kW-year to 2025 dollars using the Consumer Price Index for All Urban Consumers [@fred_ConsumerPriceIndexAll_2025], yielding **$19.65/kW-year**.[^cpi-2026-partial]

[^cpi-2026-partial]: The 2026 CPI value is a partial-year average; the deflation factor is 0.974.

**Step 3: Peak-hour identification.** We loaded hourly load for the ISO-NE Connecticut load zone for calendar year 2025 [@isone_ISONEWebServices_2025], ranked all 8,760 hours by load, and selected the **top `{python} mc.n_peak_hours` hours** as the constrained hours — all of which fall in `{python} month_list(mc.production_peak_months)`.

**Step 4: Load-weighted allocation.** We allocated the annualized cost across those 100 hours proportional to each hour's share of total load in the peak window:

$$
w_h = \frac{L_h}{\sum_{k \in \text{top-100}} L_k}
$$

Multiplying $19.65/kW-year by each hour's weight gives that hour's marginal cost in $/kWh; all remaining hours are zero. The resulting hourly profile is @fig-mc-heatmap-dist-sub-tx.

**Sensitivity to load year.** The top-`{python} mc.n_peak_hours` allocation is mildly sensitive to the choice of load year. We ran the same peak-hour selection for `{python} min(mc.load_years)` through `{python} max(mc.load_years)` and found that all peak hours fall within `{python} month_list(mc.peak_month_cols)` in every year (@tbl-peak-hour-sensitivity). The month-by-month mix shifts from year to year, but `{python} month_list([mc.always_peak_month])` carries `{python} pct(mc.always_peak_month_share_min)`–`{python} pct(mc.always_peak_month_share_max)` of the peak hours in every year, and the resulting hourly marginal cost profile is qualitatively the same across all four years.

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| output: asis

cols = mc.peak_month_cols
header = "| Load year | " + " | ".join(cols) + " |"
align = "|----------:|" + "|".join(["----:"] * len(cols)) + "|"
rows = [
    "| " + str(year) + " | " + " | ".join(mc.peak_share_cells[year]) + " |"
    for year in mc.load_years
]
caption = (
    ": Share of top-" + str(mc.n_peak_hours)
    + " peak hours by month, ISO-NE Connecticut zone, by load year."
    + " {#tbl-peak-hour-sensitivity}"
)
print("\n".join([header, align, *rows, "", caption]))
```

**Limitation.** The ISO-NE Connecticut zone load covers both Eversource and United Illuminating; no comparable MCOS exists for United Illuminating, so this schedule applies to Eversource only.
